In one sentence: the app keeps sweeping your bands with a tinySA, compares what it sees with your frequency list, and warns you as soon as a transmitter goes quiet or a signal shows up where it should not.
Part A — Getting started

1. How to read this manual

This manual is written for someone who has never done RF as well as for a technician who wants the details of a setting. It is organised in five parts:

PartFor whom / when
A. Getting startedInstall, plug in, understand the screen, find help (tutorials, glossary). Read once.
B. Understanding RFThe basics (dBm, noise, intermodulation…) and how to read the spectrum. If you are a beginner, this is what will save you the most time.
C. The festival step by stepThe complete workflow, in order: from preparing at home to the report after the last gig. It is the heart of the manual: follow it the first time.
D. Tool referenceEach tool in detail: what it is for, every setting, the pitfalls. Look it up when you need it.
E. HelpFAQ, troubleshooting, A-to-Z glossary, shortcuts, where your files are.
In the app too: the 🎓 Tutorial button offers six guided tours (discover the screen, first show from A to Z, reading the spectrum, coordinating, several stages, during the show); each step shows the part of the screen concerned and explains what it is / why / how, with a « Do it » button that opens the tool. The 📚 Glossary (☰ More › Help) explains every word.

Words in bold between quotes (« ▶ Start », « 📶 Bands »…) are the exact button texts; ☰ More › Tool means « open the ☰ More menu, then click Tool ».

2. What is it?

TinySA Monitor does two jobs at once:

  • Spectrum analyser: live spectrum over several bands, max hold, waterfall, live zoom, venue reference curve, TV channel guide and allocations per country.
  • Frequency monitor: 100+ frequencies, each with a status (“must transmit” or “must stay free”). The app works out the state of each one, raises alarms (sound, panel, phone), keeps a log and can record the whole session so you can look at it again after the show.

On top of that: basic coordination tools (plan check, intermodulation, backup frequency, line check), a web page for the team, alerts on phones.

TinySA Monitor is a monitor, not coordination software. Its calculations (spacing, intermod, filter) are for checking and troubleshooting on site from the measured spectrum. To build your frequency plan, use a dedicated tool, far more complete (Shure Wireless Workbench, Sennheiser WSM, Soundbase…), then import the plan here to monitor it during the show.
The band allocations shown (DTT, 4G/5G, aero…) are for guidance only: always check the local regulations (Ofcom, ANFR, BNetzA…) before transmitting.

3. The equipment

What you need at minimum

  • A tinySA Ultra (the « Ultra » model, with the big screen, up to 6 GHz). It is a small spectrum analyser: a device that measures radio power frequency by frequency. The app tells it what to measure and fetches the results over USB.
  • Its antenna (supplied), screwed onto the RF socket. For mics (470–700 MHz), the telescopic antenna or a small UHF antenna is enough. An antenna for the wrong band sees badly: the measured level is lower than reality.
  • A USB-C cable that carries data. Careful: many USB-C cables only charge. If the PC does not see the tinySA, change the cable first.
  • A Windows PC (10 or 11). No need for a racing machine; a screen of at least 1280 × 720.

Optional

  • A 2nd tinySA: twice as fast (they share the bands), or one per stage (chapter « Two tinySAs, network relay »).
  • A Raspberry Pi (Pi 4 recommended) + a USB power bank: the « roaming tinySA » kit to scan each stage or hunt a jammer while the PC stays at the FOH. The software kit comes with each version (relais-raspberry-pi.zip).
  • A phone: to receive alarms (ntfy, Telegram) and see the web page (list, wall, spectrum, FOH, hunt, field).
  • A 2nd screen: for the frequency wall at the FOH.
  • A small Wi-Fi router: your own network for the PC, the Pi and the phones, more reliable than a venue's Wi-Fi.
Where to put the tinySA? Like a mic receiver: high up, in the clear, near the receiving antennas but not right next to a transmitter (a transmitter 10 cm away saturates the measurement and shows fake signals). Away from LED screens, power supplies and computers, which raise the noise floor.

4. Install and start

Getting the exe

  1. On the Releases page of the GitHub repository, download TinySA-Monitor.exe from the latest version (or from the “Test” pre-release to try new features).
  2. Double-click it. Windows may show “Windows protected your PC” (unsigned exe): More info › Run anyway.
  3. No installation: the exe runs as it is. Your settings are kept in %APPDATA%\TinySAMonitor\.

First start

  1. Plug the tinySA Ultra in over USB and close tinySA-App if it is open (only one program at a time on the port).
  2. At the top, pick the Port: the one marked ✔ tinySA is detected automatically. No tinySA at hand? Tick Demo mode: simulated signals so you can try everything.
  3. Click ▶ Start. The app offers to record the session (chapter 31); then the spectrum fills up and the tinySA version is shown next to the port.
Three display levels (☰ More › 👁 Display): 🟢 Ultra simple (on the very first start) = the spectrum, your list and the alarms, nothing else; 🔵 Simple = + essential settings, the log and sorting by scene / group; 🎛 Expert = every setting (RBW, LNA, attenuator, segments, measurement window, calibration…).
🎓 Tutorial (button on the home bar, or ☰ More › Help): six guided tours for beginners (see the chapter « Tutorials, glossary and tooltips »). Start with « 🖥 Discover the screen ».

5. The main window

The home bar: three steps and one sentence

At the top of the screen, three large cards, in order. The one to do now is outlined:

  1. ① The tinySA: is it plugged in? “🔌 Choose…” to say where (USB, network / Raspberry Pi), or demo mode to try without a device.
  2. ② My mics: how many frequencies are in your list; 📥 Import your plan, ＋ Add by hand, or 📡 From the scan.
  3. ③ Monitor: ▶ Start / ■ Stop, ✅ Ready? (check everything before the show) and 🖥 Show mode (full screen).

Below, one big sentence always says where you are: what is left to do, then during the show “✔ All good — 12 mics OK · 2 free reserves” (green), “✔ No alarm — 1 mic with no signal yet” (orange) or “⚠ 2 problems — HF 3: ABSENT…” (red). The ✕ hides the home bar; ☰ More › 👁 Display › 🏠 Home brings it back. In expert mode, the port choice and ▶ Start also come back in the top bar.

The sentence never says “All good” without a recent measurement: right after ▶ Start, “⏳ First sweep in progress”; if nothing arrives any more, “⚠ Degraded monitoring: no measurement for … s” (red); if some frequencies are outside the swept bands, “⚠ Partial monitoring”; if the app cannot check its measurements (internal error), “⚠ Monitoring state unknown” (red, never “OK”). Show mode and the web Control-room view show the same. Looking for a tool? 🔎 at the top (or Ctrl+K): type a word (“backup”, “relay”, “RBW”…) then Enter.

If the tinySA has a problem (not found, port already used by tinySA-App, “USB storage” mode, network relay that does not answer…), a sheet opens: what is happening, what to do step by step, and buttons ↻ Try again, 🎭 Try demo mode and 🩺 Diagnostics; it also states the consequence (e.g. “monitoring is stopped: your mics are NOT monitored”). Closed too fast? The ❓ What to do? button on card ① opens it again. In simple mode, a few technical words are replaced by everyday words (“Peak hold” for max hold, “Clear peaks” for Reset max); the technical term stays in the tooltip and comes back in expert mode.

Part B — Understanding RF

7. RF basics

You don't need to be an engineer, but these few ideas avoid 90 % of the bad surprises.

dBm: the received power

  • dBm measures a power relative to 1 milliwatt, on a logarithmic scale: 0 dBm = 1 mW, −30 dBm = 1 µW, −90 dBm = 1 picowatt.
  • +3 dB = twice the power, +10 dB = ten times, +20 dB = a hundred times. A signal at −50 dBm is 1,000 times stronger than one at −80 dBm.
  • Orders of magnitude with a decent antenna: wireless mic a few metres away −30 to −50 dBm, at 30 m −60 to −75 dBm; tinySA noise floor −100 to −110 dBm; DTT from a distant transmitter −60 to −80 dBm.
  • Other units in the app (⚙ Settings › Thresholds and alarms › Unit): dBµV = dBm + 107 (50 Ω), % like Sennheiser WSM (0 % = −120 dBm, 100 % = 0 dBm). Files always stay in dBm.

The noise floor (the “carpet”)

Even with no transmitter, the tinySA sees a minimum level: its own noise plus the venue's (LED walls, power supplies, Wi-Fi…). A signal is only usable if it clearly stands out of that carpet: that's the signal-to-noise ratio. A mic receiver typically needs 20 to 30 dB above the noise for clean audio. That's why the “busy” threshold is set a few dB above the carpet.

RBW (resolution bandwidth)

The tinySA doesn't measure one exact frequency but a small slice around it: that's the RBW.

  • Wide RBW (e.g. 300 kHz): fast sweep, but the carpet rises and close carriers merge.
  • Narrow RBW (e.g. 10 kHz): lower carpet, fine separation, but a slower sweep.
  • A narrow signal (analogue mic) reads the same whatever the RBW; a wide signal (DTT, Spectera, wideband digital mic) reads lower with a narrow RBW (you only see a slice of it). Always compare measurements made with the same settings.

Analogue, digital, wide blocks

  • Analogue FM mic: a narrow spike (≈ 200 kHz used).
  • Digital mic (ULX-D, Axient D, EW-DX…): a small rounded hump, 200 to 400 kHz wide.
  • DTT / DVB-T2, Spectera / WMAS: a 6 to 8 MHz plateau, flat on top.

Intermodulation (IM)

When several transmitters arrive strongly in a non-linear circuit (receiver front end, antenna amplifier, in-ear combiner, transmitters too close together), they create new frequencies:

  • 3rd order, 2 transmitters: 2A − B and 2B − A (the strongest and most common). E.g. A = 600, B = 602 → products at 598 and 604 MHz.
  • 3rd order, 3 transmitters: A + B − C (weaker).
  • 5th order: 3A − 2B… (weaker still, useful for in-ears on a combiner).

The stronger and the closer together the transmitters are, the stronger the products. The aim is to keep products off the frequencies in use: that's what coordination does (chapter 25).

Selectivity and receiver filter

Every receiver has an input filter that only lets through a slice of spectrum around its frequency (16 MHz, 32 MHz…). Transmitters outside it are attenuated and don't create IM in that receiver. Details in chapter 26.

Antennas, cables, distance

  • The level read depends on the antenna (gain, orientation), the cable (loss: ~3 to 6 dB per 10 m of RG58 at UHF), any amplifier / splitter and the distance. The offset (expert mode) corrects for this.
  • Put the tinySA antenna where the receiver antennas are: you see what they see.
  • A tinySA too close to a strong transmitter overloads (around −10 dBm) and shows fake signals (its own IM): move it away or add attenuation.

❓ Traces button above the spectrum: every line explained, with its settings in the same place (they are linked to the main window's settings).

Other tools: View (all bands or one), 🔍 Live zoom (tight, fast sweep around one frequency), Persistence (older sweeps as a glow, like an analyser: what comes back often shines), 📷 Capture (PNG image), right-click on the spectrum (add to my list, where could it come from, zoom).

  • 📶 Bands (next to « View »): which bands the tinySA sweeps. « Sweep all bands », or check / uncheck the ones you want, or « 🎯 Only sweep the band shown in View »: pick a band in View and the tinySA only does that one (much faster). ⚠ Frequencies in bands that are not swept are no longer monitored (no alarm for them): go back to « all » during the show.
  • 🔍 Live zoom, automatic points: when you zoom in, the app uses fewer points (one every ~10 kHz, 290 at most, never more than your bands' points): fine enough to see a mic carrier, and the sweep stays fast. The status bar shows « Zoom: width · points (step) ». Expert mode: « Points in zoom » forces a fixed number.
  • 🎯 Markers: two movable markers M1 / M2, more precise than the mouse: type the frequency to the kHz, or wheel / arrows with the chosen step (1 kHz to 1 MHz), or drag the line. « ⤒ Peak » puts M1 on the highest signal within ±0.5 MHz. Shown: level, M1 → M2 difference (kHz, dB) and occupied bandwidth around the peak (at −X dB). The button shows / hides them.
  • Click a frequency in your list: it stands out on the spectrum (amber band, thick line, name + level). Several selected rows = several highlights. If it's outside the view, the status bar says so (double-click its level to zoom onto it).

9. TV bands and channels by country

When you pick the show country (show info window, or ⚙ Settings › Country), the app uses that country's mic UHF band, its TV channels (strips under the spectrum, 📺 DTT channels) and its notes. Everything is indicative: the rule that counts is the national regulator's, to be checked before every tour. Research done in November 2026.

Swept, allowed, occupied: three different things

  • Swept: what the tinySA measures (the "UHF …" band in your bands to sweep). It can be wider than what is permitted: measuring is not transmitting, and seeing what is next door is useful.
  • Allowed: the ranges where a mic or IEM may transmit in the country, with their gaps (for example 608–614 MHz in Germany) and their conditions (licence, indoors, limited slots). They are written under the country note, in ⚙ Settings › Country.
  • Occupied: what the measurement shows here and now (thresholds, measured DTT channels).

The backup frequency, coordination and "Check the plan" only suggest frequencies inside the country's allowed ranges (box "Backup and coordination: only in the country's allowed bands", ticked by default). "✅ Ready for the show?" flags a transmitter of your list outside these ranges, or in a conditional range. These ranges stay indicative: the rule that counts is the regulator's.

Each suggested frequency carries its label: nothing when it is in a range without condition, otherwise "⚠ licensed: get the authorisation before transmitting", "indoors only", "limited use". A country without a list, or the box unticked, gives "⚠ unknown regulations / not checked": missing data never counts as an authorisation. The "Mics allowed" tooltip also gives the official texts quoted (ARCEP decisions, BNetzA Verfügungen, OFCOM RIR…) and the known uncertainties.

Where these ranges come from, and in which order they are trusted: 1) the country's regulator; 2) the official CEPT table for Europe; 3) the ITU-R international PMSE database (ITU-R ENG/PMSE, version 09/2026), very handy to compare countries but sometimes coarser (it has no 608–614 MHz column, and for Switzerland it says "licensed" while the Swiss OFCOM describes these bands as licence-free). In the app, hover the "Mics allowed" line in ⚙ Settings › Country: each range is shown with its condition, the power given by the source, the sources and the check date (November 2026).

European countries: from the official CEPT table, filled in by each regulator (CEPT EFIS – national conditions for audio PMSE).

Bands shared with IoT (LoRaWAN)

Sensors (meters, car parks, weather…) transmit in short bursts, without warning, in open-access bands. The strips under the spectrum show them: in Europe 433.05–434.79 MHz and 865–870 MHz (LoRaWAN EU863-870: 867.1–868.5 and 869.525 MHz; the 863–865 MHz mic band is not inside), in the United States and Canada 902–928 MHz (uplink 902–915, downlink 923–928), in Australia and New Zealand 915–928 MHz, in Japan 920–923.5 MHz. "✅ Ready for the show?" flags (for info) a transmitter of your list placed in one of these bands. Source: The Things Network, LoRaWAN plans by country.

Working out a channel

  • Europe, UK, New Zealand (8 MHz): channel n runs from 470 + 8 × (n − 21) to 8 MHz higher. Channel 21 = 470–478, channel 38 = 606–614, channel 48 = 686–694.
  • US, Canada (6 MHz): channel n starts at 470 + 6 × (n − 14). Channel 14 = 470–476, channel 36 = 602–608.
  • Australia (7 MHz): channel n starts at 526 + 7 × (n − 28). Channel 28 = 526–533, channel 51 = 687–694.
  • Japan (6 MHz): channel n starts at 470 + 6 × (n − 13). Channel 13 = 470–476, channel 52 = 704–710.
A country not in the list uses the European plan (470–694 MHz). For Brazil, Mexico, India, South Africa… check with the regulator (Anatel, IFT, WPC, ICASA) and add your band in ⚙ Settings › Bands to sweep.
Part C — The festival step by step

10. Overview: the steps of a festival

Here is the complete flow. Each step has its own chapter right after, with the detailed clicks.

WhenStepResult
Weeks before, at home1. Prepare: bands, country, list of your devices, profiles, stages, show 🎪A show file ready, the app known (demo mode)
Arriving on site2. Scan the venue: let the tinySA sweep each placeYou know what already occupies the air
Arriving (several stages)3. Scan each stage with the roaming tinySAOne or more scans kept per stage, on the PC
Load-in4. Build the plan: coordination per stage or global, check, intermod, statusesA clean frequency list, without conflicts
Before doors5. Prepare monitoring: thresholds, alarms, line check, alerts, web page, wallEverything checked, the team sees the state
Show6. Monitor and reactProblems are seen and fixed in time
Night, several days7. Keep it running: festival modeAuto restart, summary every morning
After8. Review, report, keepReport, replay, show reusable next year

The « new show » assistant

🧭 Assistant (on the home bar, or first in 📋 Prepare, and by itself after « New show ») walks you through, in order: 1. the show (name, country, venue postcode), 2. your mics (import, paste, add), 3. scan the venue (5 minutes recommended, elapsed time shown), 4. DTT channels (« Measure and grey out »), 5. ready for the show (check, start, Show mode). Each step says why and how, with the buttons that do it; ✓ = done. You can skip a step, come back, and keep working in the app while the assistant is open.

The app suggests what's next

A discreet banner above the spectrum suggests the next move at the right time: after 5 minutes of scan, « N DTT channels found: grey them? »; if monitoring runs with an empty list, « add from the scan or import? »; when the country adjusts the band, « band adjusted to 470–608 MHz » with Cancel. ✕ = don't suggest again for this show.

The spectrum legend

At the top left of the spectrum: Live · Peak hold · Threshold (auto) · DTT · My mics, in their colours. Clicking a chip = what it is and what to do (clear peaks, how the auto threshold works, see DTT channels, choose markers…). The main windows have a ❓ Manual button that opens the right chapter.

Small event, a single stage? Do steps 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8; it takes about an hour.

11. Step 1 — Prepare at home

1.1 Learn the app in demo mode

  1. Start the app, tick Demo mode (at the top) then ▶ Start. Fake signals appear: mics, TV channels, a jammer that comes and goes.
  2. Do the 🎤 My first show, from A to Z tutorial (🎓 Tutorial). It walks you through each step with the fake signals.
  3. Untick demo mode when you are done (■ Stop first).

1.2 Country and bands

  1. In the settings, Country and plan section: choose your country. It sets the TV channels shown and the « what is this frequency used for » strip under the spectrum.
  2. Bands to sweep: only keep the ranges where your devices are. Classic example: UHF 470–694 MHz for mics and in-ears; add 1.8 GHz (DECT) or 2.4 GHz if you have those systems. Fewer bands = faster sweep = more reactive alarms.
  3. ⚡ Points above the spectrum: leave Auto balanced. The app picks the fineness so a sweep stays fast.

1.3 Your frequency list

If you already have a plan (.ezrf3, WWB, WSM, Excel), 📋 Prepare › 📥 Import. Otherwise, add by hand (＋ Add) or wait for the site scan to do the coordination (step 4).

For each frequency, the status is the most important setting:

  • « In use » (must transmit): your transmitter must be on it. If it disappears → ABSENT alarm.
  • « Free » (must stay free): a reserve (backup, another day). If someone comes onto it → CONFLICT alarm.

1.4 Device profiles

📋 Prepare › 🎛 Device profiles: pick the brand / range of each device. The profile gives the minimum spacing between frequencies, the receiver filter width and the tuning step. Coordination calculations depend on it. If you know the values from your usual coordination software, create a custom profile with them.

1.5 Stages (festival)

In « My frequencies », Sort by stage › group box: ＋ Stage for each stage (Main stage, Club…), ＋ Group for each family (Mics, In-ears, Walkies…). Put your frequencies in them (right-click a stage › assign the selection). The alarm priority is set per group (right-click › 🔔 Priority).

1.6 Save the show

Ctrl+S (or 🎪 Shows › Save): a .tsashow file keeps everything (frequencies, stages, bands, kept scans, schedule). Fill in the festival name, venue and dates (🎪 › Show info): they will appear in the reports.

1.7 The preparation file

📋 Prepare › 🖨 Preparation file: a PDF sheet to print or send to the production and the other RF teams. It contains the venue spectrum (kept scans + max hold), the frequency plan per stage › group (status, device, what is paused), the country regulation with what is left to check frequency by frequency, the DTV channels, the list of scans with their RBW and, if the coordination tools are shown, the plan check. Choose “Web page (*.html)” in the save window for a version to open in a browser.

12. Step 2 — Arriving on site: scan the venue

Why? Before choosing any frequency, you need to know what already occupies the air: TV channels, other RF teams (rental companies, broadcast, security), walkie-talkies, LED screens that « spit ». A frequency that looks free on paper may be taken on site.

  1. Set up the tinySA where your receivers will be (RF desk, side-stage), antenna in the clear.
  2. Choose the port (✔ tinySA) then click 📋 Prepare › ▶ Scan here: sweeping starts and the max hold (orange curve) restarts from zero.
  3. Let it run at least 10 minutes, ideally during light / screen tests (they change the noise floor). The longer, the more the max hold catches intermittent transmitters (walkies, transmitters being tested).
  4. Look at the spectrum (chapter « Reading the spectrum »): 8 MHz plateaus = TV, peaks = transmitters, the bottom = noise floor. Hover to read frequency and level.
  5. Keep this scan: 📋 Prepare › 📍 Scans by location › 📍 Keep (name it after the stage or place). It will be used for coordination and the report.
  6. Optional: 📏 Reference › Capture = the venue's « quiet », for a relative threshold (expert).

The scan for coordination, done automatically

📋 Prepare › 📏 Scan for coordination makes the “clean” scan a coordination software expects: fine RBW (30 kHz recommended), points matched to that RBW (no signal falls between two points), peaks cleared then kept for the chosen time (5 minutes by default); at the end the scan is filed in Scans by location with its RBW, in the chosen stage. Your monitoring settings (RBW, points, max hold) come back as before by themselves. The sweep is slower during this scan (many more points): that's normal. ■ Stop (keep nothing) cancels and puts everything back.

The venue's DTT channels

📋 Prepare › 📺 Local DTT channels and nearby transmitters answers « which channels does TV use here? » from your scan, without internet:

  • Channels measured here: each channel (21 to 48 in France, 8 MHz) is classified 📺 DTT (flat plateau well above the noise), other signal (something narrow: mic, carrier), free or not measured (outside your bands). « Plateau from » sets the margin above the noise (10 dB by default). DTT channels are greyed « TNT n » on the spectrum (checkbox); « Copy » pastes the table into an email or a spreadsheet. You know the area better than the measurement? Double-click a channel (automatic → DTT → free → automatic) or right-click several: your « by hand » choice overrides the measurement, is kept with the show and greyed again when it opens, even without a scan. Importing an .ezrf3 plan? Its active TV channels are greyed « DTT (plan) » too, and updated automatically if you follow the file. On tour, ↺ New venue sets everything back to automatic (by-hand choices and plan channels forgotten), or resets everything and clears the peak hold to rescan; importing a new plan with « Replace my list » also replaces the old plan's TV channels.
  • Nearby transmitters (ANFR), optional: the open ANFR database (data.gouv.fr) lists DTT transmitters in France with their position. Download it once (≈ 65 MB, 0.3 MB stays on the PC) or import the files if you already have them, then type the show venue (postcode or « latitude, longitude »): the app lists nearby DTT sites (distance, number of multiplexes, height, operator) and warns if a big transmitter is very close (very strong DTT, keep a margin). The database does not give each transmitter's channels: the measured channels are what counts. The venue is kept with the show.
Classic trap: scanning at 9 am on an empty site, then finding out in the evening that the regional TV is setting up its links. Scan again once the other teams have arrived, and compare (⚖ in the replay).

13. Step 3 — Several stages: scan each place with the roaming tinySA

Why? On a big site, each stage has its own radio environment: the stage near the road sees the town's TV transmitter, the one in the tent sees the LED screens. By keeping a scan per stage, you can coordinate each stage with its spectrum, or the whole site at once.

3.1 The kit

A tinySA plugged into a Raspberry Pi with a power bank, in a bag, linked over Wi-Fi to the FOH PC. Full setup in the chapter « Two tinySAs, network relay › Portable hunting kit » (install once, relais-raspberry-pi.zip file supplied with each version). With a single tinySA, it is the 1st tinySA (port list › « 🌐 Network tinySA… » › the Pi's address). With two, the 2nd.

3.2 Prepare the web page

  1. On the PC: 📣 Alerts and web page (🎚 Monitor) › web page tab: enable it, set a PIN code (4 digits or more) and tick the 🎒 Field view (it is hidden by default).
  2. The page's address is shown (e.g. http://192.168.1.10:8080): open it on your phone, connected to the same Wi-Fi.

3.3 Walking around the site

  1. Arrive at the first stage. On the phone, 🎒 Field view: choose the bag's tinySA, tick the stage you are at then 📡 This tinySA is here. (Several neighbouring stages? tick them all.)
  2. ↺ New scan here: those stages' max hold restarts from zero.
  3. Look at 📈 What the tinySA sees: the live spectrum, the persistence (blue traces that fade: what comes back often makes a thick line) and the stage's max hold in its colour. Wait until the max hold stops moving much (a few minutes).
  4. 💾 Keep this scan, with a label if you like (« front », « stage left », « FOH »). You can keep several per stage, at different spots: they will be merged.
  5. Move to the next stage and start again. Everything is saved on the PC, in the show.

On the PC, clicking a stage in « My frequencies » shows the merge of its scans (dashes); 📋 Prepare › 📍 Scans by location lists them all, and lets you export them (WWB, WSM, CSV) or import a scan from other software (including WWB's native .sdb3 format).

14. Step 4 — Build the frequency plan

The plan is built in your coordination software (WWB, WSM, Soundbase…): then import it here (② My mics › 📥 Import). The tools described below (check, coordinate, intermod) are basic coordination, hidden by default: ⚙ Settings › General › “Coordination tools (advanced)”. The 🆘 backup frequency is always available.

The goal: a list where each frequency is far enough from the others, with no « ghost frequency » (intermodulation) on it, and away from what already occupies the venue.

4.1 Choose the profiles

Each frequency has its device (« Device » column of 🧮 Check the plan): spacing and filter depend on it (chapter « Receiver filter and device profiles »).

4.2 Find frequencies: auto coordination

  1. 📋 Prepare › 🪄 Find N compatible frequencies.
  2. Device: the profile of the equipment to tune. How many: the number of frequencies. From … to: the range of your transmitters (written on them, e.g. 470–608 MHz for an « A » range).
  3. Avoid what is busy + the « Spectrum: … » list:
    • stage X: per-stage coordination (its kept scans + its current max hold); offered by default if that stage is selected in « My frequencies », and the new frequencies are filed in it;
    • whole site: global coordination (merge of all scans): for equipment that moves between stages, or a compact site;
    • current max hold: what the tinySAs see now.
  4. Busy if: when a frequency of that spectrum counts as busy. Auto (recommended) = noise floor of THIS spectrum + a margin (15 dB by default); next to it, the app shows the resulting threshold and the share of the spectrum above it. Why not your monitoring threshold? The max hold keeps hours of noise peaks, well above the current noise: compared with the auto threshold (current noise + 13 dB), almost everything looked busy. Other choices: My “busy” threshold (the one in the threshold bar) or a fixed threshold.
  5. Scan: the RBW (measurement resolution) of the avoided spectrum. For coordination, use a fine RBW, 30 kHz or less: a wide RBW spreads narrow signals and raises the noise (from 100 to 30 kHz, noise and DTV drop by about 5 dB, a mic hardly at all), and the “busy” threshold no longer means the same thing. The app warns when the RBW is too wide, unknown (imported scan) or different between scans; the RBW 30 kHz button sets it in one click (then redo the scan). Each kept scan records its RBW (scan info, site report, exported file name: “…_RBW30k.csv”).
  6. 🔎 Search, then ＋ Add to my list. They arrive with the « In use » status.

If the app does not find enough (« the range is full »), it is often physics: too many transmitters on too few MHz. Widen the range, choose a more robust profile (tighter spacing and tolerances), or spread over another band.

4.3 Check

📋 Prepare › 🧮 Check the plan checks the whole list. Each line marked ✗ says why (« too close to HF 3 », « IM3 of HF 1 and HF 4 »); Replace suggests a frequency that creates no new problem. Check again until there are 0 problems.

4.4 Understand intermod

📋 Prepare › ⚡ Intermodulation lists the products (2A − B, A + B − C…) landing on your frequencies, from the most serious (measured above the threshold) to the least (calculation only). The rules at the top choose what is counted; « Standard » (2 TX ±100 kHz, 3 TX ±50 kHz) is a good starting point.

4.5 Reserves

Keep 2 or 3 compatible frequencies as « Free » per stage: they will be your backups, and the app warns you if someone moves onto them.

4.6 Set the transmitters and save

Export the list (📋 Prepare › 📤 Export) to set the receivers (or their software), then Ctrl+S.

15. Step 5 — Before doors open

  1. 🎚 Monitor › ⚡ Quick presets: pick your situation (🎪 outdoor festival, 🎭 venue, 🌙 overnight monitoring, 🔭 site survey). The window shows what will change before you apply; everything stays adjustable afterwards.
  2. Thresholds (threshold bar above the spectrum): keep Auto pressed (the default): each frequency gets its own threshold, just above its noise floor, and it follows the noise on its own. « Weak level from »: 10 dB below busy. « TX absent after »: 5 to 10 s.
  3. 🎚 Monitor › ▶ Start monitoring; accept to record the session.
  4. 🎤 Line check (Ctrl+L): switch the transmitters on one by one; each frequency seen gets ticked. An « unknown » frequency near a missing one = the wrongly set transmitter.
  5. All « In use » lines must be OK (green). The « Free » ones blue.
  6. 📣 Phone alerts: test sending (📖 Tutorial button for ntfy or Telegram).
  7. Web page for the team: 🎛 FOH view on a tablet, 📋 List on phones.
  8. 🧱 Wall on the FOH's 2nd screen (⛶ full screen).
  9. 🎬 Schedule: if sets change, enter who plays when: mics switched off between two gigs will not trigger an alarm.

16. Step 6 — During the show: monitor and react

The Signal column and the wall are enough to follow along: green = all is well. When an alarm goes off (sound + red line in the alarms + phone):

AlarmWhat it meansWhat to do, in order
ABSENTAn « In use » transmitter is no longer seen1. Battery? transmitter on, not in RF mute? 2. Antenna bent / unplugged? 3. Artist out of range (dressing rooms, car park)? 4. Planned changeover → schedule. Acknowledge to stop the sound.
CONFLICTA signal on a « Free » frequency1. Look at the spectrum: narrow peak (transmitter) or wide bump (noise)? 2. « seen by … » and « INTERMOD » info: if it is an intermod product, the formula is given. 3. If it was your reserve, it can no longer be used: 🆘 find another one. 4. 🔎 Hunt to find the source.
TOO STRONGA huge signal somewhereA transmitter right next to the tinySA (false alarm), or a powerful jammer: hunt.
DEVICEThe tinySA no longer answersCable, tinySA battery, Pi Wi-Fi. The app retries by itself; after 3 failures, unplug / replug.
weak (no alarm)Signal present but lowDistant transmitter or battery running low: keep an eye on it.

A mic gets jammed in the middle of a gig

The fastest: 🆘 Replace this mic (right-click the mic in the list, its wall or Show-mode tile, or the alarm, button in the alarm panel, or 🆘 on the phone's 🛠 Tech page). The app suggests 3 frequencies that are free according to the measurement, compatible with your whole plan, with the settings of the mic's device and inside its band. If nothing passes with all your rules, it says so in orange and suggests frequencies checked in 2A − B only. One click replaces the frequency in the list and logs it (“NEW FREQUENCY”); you still have to tune the transmitter AND the receiver. For a detailed search:

  1. 🆘 Backup frequency: the app suggests frequencies that are free NOW and compatible (choose the stage's spectrum). Also choose the device: its settings are used and, if its range is known (imported plan, profile with a range), the search never leaves that range.
  2. Switch the transmitter / receiver pair (or take a « Free » reserve already prepared).
  3. Change the frequency in the list (double-click MHz): the log notes « NEW FREQUENCY ».
  4. After the song: 🔎 hunt to find the culprit.

17. Step 7 — The night and several days

🎚 Monitor › 🌙 Festival mode: the app

  • restarts monitoring by itself after a power cut or a crash (if it was running);
  • prevents the PC from going to sleep;
  • can start with Windows;
  • sends a summary every morning (phone + HTML report): the night's alarms, or « ✅ all good ».

Keep the tinySA on mains power (not on its battery). Check disk space if session recording is on (a few tens of MB per hour, shown in the settings).

18. Step 8 — After the festival

  1. ■ Stop: the session is closed (folder with the recorded spectrum, the log and the list).
  2. 📊 Analyse › ⏪ Replay: review any moment (time slider); « 📂 Open a session » for another day; ⚖ compare two sessions.
  3. 📊 Occupancy per hour: the time slots when each frequency was disturbed.
  4. 📄 Show report: a clean HTML document (frequencies, alarms, incidents, scans) to send to the production.
  5. 🔁 Recurring disturbances (📊 Analyse): reads several days of automatic logs and lists what comes back at the same time (± 20 minutes by default) on at least 2 days: “UNKNOWN · Walkie (446.006 MHz): 3 days out of 3 around 19:03”. A “must transmit” mic being present is not a disturbance (that's normal); its drop-outs (MISSING) are counted. Double-click = hunt this signal. The Auto log (CSV / day) box must be ticked (Log tab).
  6. Ctrl+S: the show keeps the per-stage scans and the plan. Next year: 🎪 › Open, and you start again from there.
Part D — Tool reference

19. Preparing a show

Bands to sweep

  • The app works out as much as it can on its own: on first launch, the country from Windows; on every new show, the info window asks for the show country: the app uses its frequency plan, sweeps that country's mic UHF band (adding or re-enabling it if needed) and puts the View straight on it (470–694 MHz in France and Europe, 470–702 in the UK, 470–608 in the US and Canada, 520–694 in Australia, 502–606 in New Zealand, 470–714 in Japan: indicative plans). Changing the country later (⚙ › Country) also adjusts the « UHF … » band made by the app; a band you made yourself is never touched. With a single swept band the waterfall shows by itself; after an import, if frequencies fall outside the swept bands, it offers to add the missing bands.
  • ⚙ Settings › Bands to sweep: tick the bands, or add some (start, stop, step). Presets exist (UHF mics, Spectera, 1G4…).
  • More points means finer detail but a longer cycle. The app estimates how long a cycle takes.
  • ⚡ Points (button in the spectrum bar, in every mode, or ⚙ Settings › Measurement › Points / sweep): ⚡ Auto fast / balanced / detailed (≈ 2,000 / 4,500 / 9,000 points per cycle) or a fixed number per band. Auto balanced is the default. In Auto, the app picks the step from the total width of your checked bands; balanced gives 10 kHz on a small area or the FM band, 50 kHz over the whole 470–694 UHF, 125 kHz over 470–960. Never finer than 10 kHz (a mic carrier is ~200 kHz wide: finer shows nothing more), and never wider than the RBW if you force it (otherwise a narrow signal could slip between two points). The step updates by itself when you add, check or uncheck a band; setting a band's points by hand turns Auto off.
  • Country and plan: pick your country for the right TV channels and allocations.

Your frequencies

  • 📡 Add from the scan (📋 Prepare): the signals the tinySA sees above a threshold (max hold, or live) become frequencies in your list, named Scan 1, Scan 2…, in the scene / group and with the status of your choice. Then rename them, sort them, or delete the noise like any other frequency. Wide plateaus (DTT…) and what is already in your list are left out (can be unticked).
  • 📥 Import: plan from .ezrf3, WWB, WSM, Excel… The import recognises the columns and suggests names. You can also drag and drop a CSV onto the window.
  • Or by hand: ＋ Add (home screen, above the list, or 📋 Prepare › ⌨ Add mics) opens quick entry: type or paste your frequencies any way you like, “HF1 558.2, HF2 574, IEM 606.5 PSM”, one per line, or a message you received (email, text, table). The text before each frequency becomes its name; 558,2 / 558.2 MHz / 558200 kHz are understood; times and phone numbers are ignored. A preview shows what will be added; choose the stage, group and status, then ＋ Add (Ctrl+Enter). Also: right-click on the spectrum › “Add to my list”.
  • Quick naming: 📋 Prepare › ✏ Name the selection (HF 1, HF 2…), or Ctrl+D to number downwards.

Statuses: the key to everything

StatusMeaningAlarm
In use (must transmit)one of your transmitters should be there ⚠ MISSING if it stays silent longer than “TX missing after”
Free (must stay free)spare, backup frequency, area to protect ⚠ CONFLICT at the slightest signal
No statusplain monitoringnone (shows busy / free)

With the keyboard: select rows, then Ctrl+E = In use, Ctrl+1…9 = status no. 1 to 9, Ctrl+0 = none. Your own statuses: ☰ More › 🎨 Appearance and language › 🏷 Statuses.

Scenes and groups (optional)

Like folders, to find your way with lots of frequencies: a scene = a venue or a stage (Main stage, Club, TV studio…), a group = an artist or a type of equipment (Vocal mics, Drum in-ears…). Not required: everything works without it (hidden in ultra simple mode).

  • Sort by scene › group box above the list. Clicking a scene or a group = only that is monitored and scanned; Global brings everything back.
  • Right-click a group: alarm priority. Critical ❗ = sound replayed until acknowledged (every 30 s by default, ⚙ Settings › Sound); Normal; Info (no sound).
  • Right-click a group: 📻 Devices of this group (optional, one or several). E.g. an “Ears” group on Shure PSM 1000 and a “Vocals” group on QLX-D: every frequency of the group takes that device (spacing, filter, tolerances) for Check the plan and Coordinate, and the device is shown next to the group name. A frequency that has its own device (“Device” column of Check the plan) keeps it. On a scene, the choice applies to all its groups. In auto coordination, picking the scene and the group takes their device automatically. With several devices, the first one ticked is used by the group's frequencies that have none of their own, and coordination prepares one batch per device.

Saving the show

🎪 Shows › Save (Ctrl+S) keeps frequencies, scenes, statuses, bands, thresholds, country, position names, custom device profiles, venue reference and details (name, venue, dates, notes). Next year: Open a show, then Save as…. A show does not touch your preferences (colours, windows, alerts, language…).

🎪 Shows › 📦 Full backup (ZIP) (also 🔌 Hardware › 📦 Send everything for troubleshooting): a single file with the show, the config without tokens or passwords, a fresh diagnostic, and the logs, reports and diagnostics of the last 7 days (not the spectrum recordings, too big). To archive after a festival, or to send when something is wrong.

📊 Analyse › 🕘 Change history: every change to your list (added, removed, frequency, name, status, stage › group), with the time and who did it: “PC”, “📱 name” for a phone's Tech page, “🔗 plan” for a followed plan, “↶ Undone”. Kept in the show; CSV export.

⧉ Duplicate (right-click a group or a stage in “My frequencies”): a copy with the colour, priority and devices, without the frequencies.

🎪 Shows › 📐 New show from a template: choose an existing show; the new one takes its structure (stages, groups and their devices, statuses, bands, thresholds, alarms, tinySAs, device profiles, presets, venue) but starts with an empty list, without scans, states, planning or followed plan. Handy for a festival that comes back every year, or a tour where only the venue changes.

Several stages, one tinySA: scans by location

📋 Prepare › 📍 Scans by place (or 📋 Prepare). At a festival with several stages, the spectrum is not the same everywhere. Carry the tinySA around:

  1. At each stage: ▶ Start, let it run a few minutes (max hold catches what transmits), then choose the location (stages are suggested, or type a name) and 📍 Keep the current scan for this location. « Add to the scan already kept »: a 2nd pass completes the first (the strongest of both).
  2. 📥 Import a scan: a WWB (CSV or native .sdb3 file), WSM, CSV… scan made with another scanner or on another day, stored in a location.
  3. All locations are overlaid (one colour each) and their merge (white dashes) = the strongest of all at each frequency: the worst case of the whole site.
  4. 💾 Export the merge (or one location) for Shure WWB, Sennheiser WSM or as CSV (spreadsheet, other coordination software): coordinate the whole site with it. Exported range: the whole scan, the area shown, one of your bands, a device profile's range, or « from … to … » by hand (same choice in Export the scan and in the scan converter).
  5. « avoid what is busy at ALL locations » box: 🪄 Find N frequencies and 🆘 Backup frequency then avoid what is busy anywhere on the site, not only where the tinySA is. 📏 Merge = reference: the merge becomes the reference curve.

Everything is in the same window, in four tabs around the list of scans:

  • The list: tick / untick a scan to show or hide it (it also leaves the merge). Click it to see its details: scene, date, scan duration, range, number of bands, step. Rename…, File under a scene… (for per-scene coordination and changes over time) and Delete. Several scans at once: Ctrl + click, Shift + click or Ctrl+A, then Del (all deleted, Ctrl+Z brings them back), Space (hide / show again), the 👁 Show button (show, hide, show only these, show all) or right-click (file under a scene, choose all scans of a scene…). A hidden scan is still kept (and in the show) but is no longer drawn, here or on the main spectrum, nor merged.
  • Compare two places: A and B on top of each other, and below the difference A − B in dB. The text lists what is seen only at A and only at B (at least 10 dB more): a local transmitter, an LED screen, a nearby control room.
  • Before → after (same tab, or 📊 Analyse › 📸 Compare before / after): keep a BEFORE scan (before switching the mics on, before a changeover), then an AFTER scan. The table lists what appeared, disappeared, got stronger or weaker (6 dB or more), with the before and after levels; double-click = show on the spectrum. Only where both scans measured: an area one of them did not sweep (unticked band, gap between two bands) is never reported as “disappeared” or “appeared”.
  • Signals of the place: the signals of the selected scan above a level (your “occupied” threshold at first), with their width (carrier or wide signal: DTT, digital block) and whether they are already in your list. “Only those seen only here” keeps what belongs to this place. ＋ Add as outside transmitters: they enter your list without a status, so without alarms, but Check the plan and Coordinate avoid them (spacing and intermod). Copy for an email or a spreadsheet.
  • Over time: a scene scanned several times (afternoon, evening, day 2): its scans from the oldest (blue) to the newest (orange), and what appeared or disappeared between the first and the last.
  • 📄 Site survey report: a page to open in the browser and print as PDF, for the production or the coordination: the table of scans, the spectrum of the whole site (merge), then each place with its spectrum, its signals and what is seen only there, and how scenes scanned several times changed. Distant bands (UHF and 2.4 GHz) are drawn side by side, without the empty space between them.

My tinySA and their scenes (expert mode)

Continuously, on the main spectrum: say which tinySA watches which stage(s). Three ways, any time, applied immediately (nothing to restart):

  • 📡 Scenes button (arrow ▾) › 📡 My tinySA and their scenes…: a grid, one column per tinySA, one row per stage; tick the boxes. A tinySA can watch one or several stages (e.g. one tinySA between two neighbouring stages);
  • right-click a stage in « My frequencies » › 📡 Watched by;
  • the arrow ▾ of the 📡 Scenes button: « 1st tinySA watches… » (check boxes).

The « My frequencies » tree shows next to each stage the tinySA watching it (« 📡 Stage »). Every sweep of a tinySA feeds the spectrum of its stages continuously, and their max hold is kept automatically every 30 s. Click a stage: the spectrum shown is that stage's, live if a tinySA watches it (dashes = its kept max), otherwise its last kept spectrum (« no tinySA here right now »). Global: all the live data, plus the merge of all locations.

Which one is which? In the grid: 👋 Identify flashes the chosen tinySA's screen orange (needs ▶ Start). 🔢 Number it stores a number inside the tinySA (deviceid command, kept even when unplugged): if the two tinySAs are ever plugged the other way round, the app recognises them and their stages follow them.

Two tinySAs at two different locations: each sweeps all bands where it is (instead of sharing them), each location has its own live spectrum, and a stage's frequencies are judged (busy, ABSENT, CONFLICT…) by the tinySA at that stage. Global = the stronger of the two (worst case).

Kept scans are saved with the show (🎪): next year, you start again with the scans of each stage.

20. Thresholds and alarms

The three live thresholds (occupied, weak, TX absent) are in the bar right above the spectrum; everything else is in ⚙ Settings › Thresholds and alarms.

Quick presets

🎚 Monitor › ⚡ Quick presets (also in ⚙ › General) sets in one go the automatic thresholds, points per sweep, persistence, the “TX absent” delay, conflict confirmation, alarm repetition, the “too strong” alert and kept peaks, for a typical situation:

PresetForIn short
🎪 Outdoor festivallots of people, walkie-talkies, TVauto thresholds noise + 12 / + 6 dB, conflict confirmed after 3 s, persistence 10
🎭 Venue / theatrequiet venue, transmitters close bymore sensitive (+ 10 / + 5 dB), detailed measurement, faster alarms
🌙 Overnight monitoringnobody at the screenfast sweep, conflict confirmed after 5 s, sound repeated every minute, no persistence (+ festival mode offered)
🔭 Site surveyfinding space before the showdetailed measurement, peaks kept, persistence 20, discreet alarms

The window lists “now → after” before applying, and ticks ✓ the preset matching your current settings. Your list, stages and bands never move.

⭐ Custom presets: set the app up the way you like, then ⭐ Save my current settings… in the same window (a name, an optional sentence). Your preset shows under the built-in ones with a ⭐; “Delete” removes it. It is kept in the app, in the saved show (it comes back when the show is opened, on any PC) and in your user profile. The show also keeps persistence, kept peaks and alarm timing.

User profiles (your preferences)

☰ More › 👤 User profiles (also in ⚙ › General): a profile is a small .tsauser file that keeps your preferences: theme and colours, display level, unit, columns, Signal column words, thresholds, alarms and sound (except the audio output, which depends on the PC), custom presets, and the window layout (window size, panel positions, separate windows and screens). It never touches the show (frequencies, stages, bands, tinySA).

  • 💾 Save my preferences…: creates (or updates) your profile in Documents › TinySA Monitor › Profils.
  • Load this profile (or double-click): your preferences come back at once, on any PC.
  • 📤 Export / 📥 Import: hand a profile to a colleague (USB stick, e-mail); everyone keeps their habits on the same machine.

Thresholds: when is it busy?

  • “Busy” threshold: above it, the frequency is busy. Set it 6 to 10 dB above the carpet. Too low = false alarms; too high = a weak interferer goes unnoticed.
  • Auto (pressed by default): no longer one threshold for the whole spectrum, but one threshold per frequency = its local noise floor + a margin (noise + 12 dB for “busy”, noise + 6 dB for “weak”, adjustable in the bar). Handy when the carpet is not flat (nearby DTT, LED screen, bottom and top of the band). The noise is learnt continuously: it drops fast, rises slowly (about 10 minutes) and never rises while a frequency is busy, so an interferer cannot “erase” its own alarm. The auto threshold is drawn dashed on the spectrum and the Threshold column shows “auto −95”. A frequency's own threshold still wins; untick Auto to go back to fixed thresholds.
  • Why the dashed curve rises on DTT (❓ button next to Auto): the auto threshold uses the local noise floor, over ± 2 MHz. In a DTT channel that local floor is the DTT itself, so the threshold becomes « DTT + 12 dB ». That is on purpose. Example: venue noise −100 dBm, DTT channel at −82 dBm; between two channels, busy from −88; in the DTT channel, busy from −70. Your mic at −55 in that channel is seen, and if it goes off, the ABSENT alarm fires. With a threshold on pure noise, the DTT alone would always be « busy »: ABSENT would never fire and a « must stay free » reserve on the DTT would be in CONFLICT all the time. The limit: in a DTT channel, a signal weaker than DTT + 12 dB is not seen (the tinySA cannot separate it from strong DTT). To know which channels DTT takes, use 📺 DTT channels, which compares against the real venue noise.
  • “Weak” level: the in-between (yellow) zone: mic far away, weak battery, distant carrier.
  • A frequency's own threshold: right-click the row › “Frequency's own threshold” (e.g. next to a DTT transmitter where the carpet is higher).
  • Expert: threshold over reference = busy if it exceeds the venue's quiet spectrum by X dB; window = width around the frequency where the level is read; occupancy = period over which the % of time busy is computed.

Alarms

Each alarm is explained in three lines under the alarm list (and as a tooltip on each row): Measured (what the tinySA really saw: level, frequency, threshold, since when — certain), Probable cause (what we deduce: a hypothesis, to be checked) and What to do (the advice). The advice also shows under the alarm in Show mode, in phone notifications and on the web page.

  • TX missing after: how many seconds without a signal before ⚠ MISSING (never less than 2 cycles).
  • “Too strong” alert (−25 dBm by default, purple line): ⚠ TOO STRONG, overload risk (walkie-talkie right next to an antenna…).
  • Sound alert: a sound when an alarm appears; critical ones replay it until acknowledged.

Alarms that don't ring for nothing

  • ⚙ Settings › Sound › Replay critical ones: every 10 s, 30 s (default), 1 min, 5 min or never.
  • CONFLICT after (3 s by default): a signal on a « must stay free » frequency must last this long before the alarm; a brief peak no longer rings. The log still records it.
  • Short beep when a frequency becomes busy: unticked by default; only real alarms make a sound.
  • 🔕 Mute (alarm panel): mutes the sound for 5, 15, 30 or 60 min, e.g. during a line check or a changeover. Alarms stay displayed and are still sent to the phone; the sound comes back by itself.
  • 📝 What to log: see chapter 32.
  • Expert: Detect unknown signals (peaks not in the list, logged as UNKNOWN).

21. During the show

  1. ▶ Start. Every sweep updates the list, the wall, the markers and the alarms.
  2. Watch the Signal column (or the wall): green “OK” for your transmitters, blue “✔ free” for your spares.
  3. An alarm? The 🔔 turns red and the Alarms panel opens. Acknowledge silences the sound but keeps the alarm (orange) as long as the problem is there.
  4. A strange signal? Right-click it: ⚡ Where could it come from? (intermod from the measured spectrum), 🔍 zoom, ＋ add to my list.
  • Live zoom: double-click a frequency's level or signal, or right-click › 🔍 Live zoom.
  • 📍 Markers: which ones to show (by state, scene, status, alarms always visible, style). Ctrl+M hides / shows them all.
  • 📏 Reference › Capture: the venue's noise floor, to be done before the audience arrives.

Festival mode (all night)

🎚 Monitor, or 🎚 Monitor › 🌙 Festival mode. To let the PC monitor on its own at night or all week:

  • Automatic resume: if the app stops while monitoring (power cut, crash, Windows restart), it restarts monitoring by itself the next time it starts, without asking (session recording follows your last choice). Closed on purpose: it restarts nothing.
  • Start with Windows: the app starts when the session opens. For a real recovery after a power cut, the PC must also power back on by itself (BIOS setting « Restore on AC power loss ») and log in without a password.
  • No sleep while monitoring (the screen may still turn off).
  • Daily summary at the chosen time: an HTML report of the events since the previous summary (logs folder › rapports) and a message on the phone (ntfy / Telegram, set in 📣 Alerts): « ✔ All good » or « ⚠ 2 active alarm(s) », with the alarms of the last 24 h, how long it has been running and the tinySAs online. If the PC was asleep at that time, the summary is done as soon as it wakes up. « 📨 Run the summary now » to test. The report starts with « At a glance »: a verdict, events hour by hour (red = alarms, orange = to look at), grouped alarms (one line per mic, from such time to such time), unstable frequencies (a weak signal right at the threshold) and changed frequencies. 📊 Analyse › 🌅 Night summary opens it at any time.
  • 🛡 Watchdog (ticked by default): a small windowless program starts the app and watches it. If it crashes, or shows no sign of life for 90 s (frozen), it closes and restarts it, and monitoring resumes where it was. Closed normally, the watchdog stops with it. If the app crashes in a loop (5 times in 10 min), the watchdog waits 5 min before trying again. The watchdog is used when starting with Windows; to get it right away: 🛡 Restart now under the watchdog. What happened is written to garde.log (configuration folder). You can also run TinySA-Monitor.exe --garde yourself (shortcut). To check it works, under the watchdog: 💥 Test: crash (the app must reopen within a few seconds and monitoring resume) and 🧊 Test: frozen app (closed then reopened after 90 s).

22. Reading the states

StatusSignal presentNo signal
Must transmitOK · “OK (weak)” “silent”, then ⚠ MISSING
Must stay free⚠ CONFLICT (or INTERMOD) ✔ free
No statusBUSY (no room here)free
  • INTERMOD: a signal on a “must stay free” frequency that matches an intermodulation product of your transmitters; the formula is in the alarm (e.g. “2×HF 1 − HF 3”).
  • ⚠ DEVICE: a tinySA dropped out (cable, frozen). The app retries on its own every 5 s.
  • ⚠ TOO STRONG: signal above the alert level, overload risk.
  • Words and colours can be changed: ☰ More › 🎨 Appearance and language › 🔤 Words and colours.

The margin: how far the signal rises above the noise

The Margin column (next to Status) says how many dB the signal rises above the noise floor around it (measured over ± 2 MHz, without the frequency itself). It says more than the raw level: −70 dBm is very good in a quiet venue and borderline in an area full of DTT.

MarginWhat it means
≥ 20 dBVery good: the mic is well above the noise.
10 to 20 dBFine.
6 to 10 dBBorderline: antenna, distance, battery? (“✅ Ready?” flags it)
less than 6 dBBuried: we cannot tell whether the transmitter is there.

On a reserve (must stay free), it is the opposite: a large margin means someone is on it.

Overload and resolution

  • Overload: if the tinySA receives a very strong signal (a transmitter right next to its antenna), its measurements become wrong (squashed levels, false signals). The home bar and “✅ Ready?” say so: move the antenna away, turn the LNA off or add attenuation (⚙ › Measurement). The thresholds (−25 / −15 dBm, 15 dB earlier with the LNA) are cautious values.
  • Resolution: two frequencies closer than twice the sweep step merge on the spectrum. “✅ Ready?” lists those pairs: use ⚡ Points › Auto detailed or a finer band step.
  • Old measurements: a frequency in a swept band but with no recent measurement is flagged (tinySA dropping out, band unticked).

23. The frequency wall

  • 🧱 button (top bar) or 🎚 Monitor › 🧱 Wall: one tile per frequency, colour = signal state.
  • 📋 Choose: which frequencies get a tile. “Alarms always visible” brings back a removed frequency while it is in alarm.
  • Tile size: Auto, or Small / Medium / Large.
  • 🗗 Detach / 📌 Dock; 🖥 Other screen; F11 = full screen, Esc to go back.

24. Windows and dual screen

☰ More › 🪟 Windows and layouts: Standard, Analyser only, Monitoring, Dual screen, and 🗗 Real windows / dual screen: each panel (Spectrum, Waterfall, List, Log, Alarms, Settings) as a real Windows window (maximise, taskbar), on the screen of your choice, maximised or full screen. In the window: 🖥 Next screen, ⛶ Full screen (F11), 📌 Dock. Windows reopen in the same place at the next start; “📌 Dock all” or the Standard layout puts everything back into the main window.

25. Coordination: plan, intermod, backup

Hidden by default. Check the plan, Coordinate, Intermod and Device profiles only appear with ⚙ Settings › General › “Coordination tools (advanced)”. The 🆘 backup frequency is always available. To build a plan, use dedicated coordination software and import it here.

Image frequency. Analogue (superheterodyne) receivers have an intermediate frequency (IF), often 10.7 MHz: a transmitter at ± IF from their frequency (589.3 and 610.7 MHz for a receiver on 600) lands on their image frequency. With an IF in the device profile (“IF (image frequency)” field, also read from .ezrf3 plans), Check the plan flags it and the suggestions avoid it. Both sides are checked, at the receiver's 2 TX tolerance (100 kHz if it is 0).

Find N compatible frequencies (auto coordination)

📋 Prepare (with the coordination tools). Like coordination software: pick the device (its filter, spacing, step, chapter 26), how many frequencies you need and the range (your transmitters' band). Method: 🎲 spread at random (default: each frequency starts from a random point in the range, the best of 3 tries is kept; much faster and better with many frequencies) or ⬆ one after the other (lowest first, everything packs at the bottom). The calculation runs in the background: the app stays usable and the button becomes "Cancel the calculation". 🪄 Search finds frequencies compatible with your whole list and with each other (spacing, intermod per the rules, filter), on the device's step, avoiding what the tinySA sees as busy (max hold above the « busy » threshold: run 📋 Prepare › ▶ Scan here for a few minutes first). ＋ Add to my list puts them « In use », named « HF 1, HF 2… », in the chosen stage. A bar shows how many frequencies are already found. If the device has a known range (imported plan, profile with a range), the search stays inside it even if you typed a wider range (the app says so). If some are missing, « What blocks » gives the share of the range taken by each cause: outside the country's allowed bands, busy according to the measurement (DTT…), too close to a plan frequency, or intermod, with advice (widen the range, a more robust device, softer rules). Then check with 🧮.

Several devices at once (coordination between devices, e.g. 8 QLX-D + 6 PSM 1000): set the device, how many, the range and the name, then ＋ Add this batch; repeat for the next device. 🪄 Search then finds the frequencies of each batch, all compatible with each other and with your list, each with the rules of its own device. Put the most demanding device first (more spacing, larger tolerances): it gets the pick of the best spots. If the chosen group has several devices (right-click the group › 📻 Devices of this group), one batch per device is prepared automatically.

Check the plan

Basic coordination: a quick check of your plan, not a replacement for your coordination software (WWB, WSM, Soundbase…), which remains the tool to build the plan.
  • 🧮 button or 📋 Prepare › 🧮 Check the plan. For each frequency: ✔ compatible or ✗ with the details (spacing too small, 2A − B, A + B − C, 5th order, image frequency, outside its device's range when the device range is known).
  • Default device and Device column: a profile per frequency (chapter 26).
  • Rules: “Standard” (2 TX ±100 kHz, 3 TX ±50 kHz) by default; the sentence “We check: …” says exactly what is counted.
  • On a ✗ row: 🔍 Suggest a compatible frequency (on the device's step, avoiding what the tinySA sees as busy, and without leaving its device's range), then ✔ Replace.

Intermodulation

  • Compute products: what lands on what among your transmitters, with the measured level and a verdict 🔴 🟠 🟡 ⚪.
  • Find the origin of a signal: the source “signals SEEN on the spectrum” (default) = the peaks actually measured (max hold), declared in your list or not. The app looks for combinations of those peaks that land on the interfering signal, most likely first (3rd order, right on it). Let the sweep run for a while first: the max hold catches intermittent transmitters.
  • 👁 Monitor adds products to your list as “Free”.

Stage schedule (who plays when)

🎚 Monitor › 🎬, or 🎚 Monitor. For each stage, you add slots: group (or the whole stage), day (every day or a specific festival day), start and end (an end before the start = the set ends after midnight). With a margin before (line check, changeover: 15 min by default) and after (encore: 10 min):

  • during its slot, the group must transmit: normal ABSENT alarm if a mic goes quiet;
  • outside its slot, its mics are « 💤 not on stage »: no more alarms for a band that hasn't arrived yet or has already left; if they transmit anyway (soundcheck), they stay « OK »;
  • each stage has its own schedule; a stage without slots is not affected;
  • every change is written to the log (« STAGE CHANGEOVER: Group A → Group B »); the web page's Control room view shows the group in grey « 💤 not on stage ».

The schedule is saved with the show (🎪).

States: switch plan in one click

Several plans in the same show (an artist, a stage, a day)? Create a state per plan: 🎚 Monitor › 📸 States, or the 📸 button at the top of “My frequencies”.

  • ＋ New starts from the frequencies monitored right now; in the table, tick those that play in this state (“Tick a stage / a group” is quick).
  • ▶ Activate (or one click in the 📸 button menu): the state's frequencies are monitored, the others become “💤 paused (state)”: no CONFLICT or ABSENT alarm, and Check the plan does not count them.
  • 🔒 Always: the frequency stays active whatever the state (intercom, walkie-talkies, FOH IEMs…).
  • A frequency added while a state is active joins that state; a moved frequency stays in its states.
  • States are saved with the show, and the 🛠 Tech page can switch state from a phone.

Schedule or states? The schedule pauses at the set time, by itself; states switch when you decide. Both can be used together.

Site map

🎚 Monitor › 🗺 Site map (or 🔌 Hardware › 🗺 Map): a real window where your stages and tinySAs are tiles to drag on a dotted grid, like a network diagram. No plan needed: the grid is enough. At the top, a slim bar: 🖼 Plan, 🔥 Heat, “⤢ Fit all” and “⋯” (grid, rearrange, export); zoom (+ / −) and the heat legend sit on the map, and messages appear in a bubble at the top.

  • Placing: the first time everything is laid out for you; drag the tiles where you want (they snap to the grid). A new stage or a new tinySA places itself to the right of the others. Wheel = zoom, drag the background = pan. “⋯ › Rearrange automatically” starts over.
  • Live: each stage lights green, orange or red from its mics and alarms; each tinySA shows whether it is online and what it watches. A line links each tinySA to the stages it watches (dashed if it is lost).
  • Drag and drop: drop a tinySA ONTO a stage to attach it. Right-click a tinySA: choose its stages, “whole site”, 👋 identify it. Double-click a stage: the list and the spectrum switch to it.
  • Background plan (optional): 🖼 Plan › Choose an image (the production plan as PNG / JPG). Opacity in the same menu; “Align the plan” to move it with the mouse (Ctrl + wheel for the size), untick to lock it.
  • Heat map: during a 🔎 interference hunt, each recorded point keeps the level measured there: blue = weak, red = where it is loudest (red circle = the strongest point). With a laptop: while the hunt runs, a simple click on the map notes the level there (the bubble at the top reminds you). With the phone: 🔎 Hunt view › “🗺 Where am I?”, tap the plan where you are. One frequency at a time (🔥 Heat › Hunted frequency), “Clear the points shown” to start again.
  • Reading aids (🔥 Heat › On the map, each can be turned off): contour lines every 5 dB (like a topographic map: where they bunch up, the level rises fast); “this way” direction: your last measurement is circled (“you are here”) and ››› chevrons with “+N dB” show where the strongest point is (the bubble at the top says how many dB you can still gain, or that you are already at the strongest); hunt route (thin trace, sharper towards the latest points, off by default). “Gradient spread”: tight if your points are close together, wide if they are far apart.
  • Appearance (🔥 Heat › Appearance): 🎨 Colours (classic blue → yellow → red, thermal camera, colour-blind purple → green → yellow, glacier, soft, or a single colour = your theme accent), Intensity (slider: lower it to see the background plan), “Levels written on the points” (unticked: only the strongest keeps its level), point size (small / medium / large), route thickness (thin / normal / thick), direction colour (theme accent, colour of the strongest point, white, orange, green). The phone follows the same colours.
  • Stage monitoring: besides the state of its mics, a stage shows “Monitoring lost” when none of its tinySAs is online, “No measurement” or “Partial measurement” when its mics have no recent measurement (grey dots): an old green never passes for working monitoring.
  • The map (positions, plan, points) is kept in the show, plan image included: the show opened on another PC gets its plan back (copied to Documents/TinySA Monitor/Plans). “⋯ › Export as PNG” to print it.

Interference hunt

🎚 Monitor, 🎚 Monitor, or right-click a row of the log. Put a directional antenna on the tinySA, choose the frequency (taken from the row selected in your list, or from M1) and ▶ Hunt: the app runs a tight live zoom (2 MHz by default, very fast sweep) and plays a beep that speeds up and rises as the level rises, like a metal detector. The level is shown in large type, with the max seen and the gap to the max (« −7.8 dB »): turn around, move, and walk back to the source. « Follow the strongest in the area » if the signal drifts a bit. If it saturates close by, add attenuation.

Transmit mode (generator)

🎚 Monitor › 📡. The tinySA Ultra becomes a small generator to test a receiver (its RF meter, its squelch, reception of a frequency), a cable or a splitter: pure carrier, FM (like an analogue mic: adjustable deviation and test tone) or AM, from −115 to about −20 dBm. « Step through my list » moves from one frequency of your list to the next every N seconds: handy to check every receiver in turn. ⚠ Cable only, with an attenuator: transmitting over the air without authorisation is illegal. Monitoring must be stopped (the tinySA can't sweep and transmit at the same time); « ■ Stop transmitting » puts it back into analyser mode.

Backup frequency

Free channels according to the measured spectrum, with no intermod against your list, one click away when a mic gets interference. Only transmitters count for intermod (not « must stay free » reserves), with the receiver filter. With many transmitters, 3 TX products quickly cover the whole band: pick « 2 TX only ». If there is no perfect frequency, the app still offers the least bad ones, in orange, with what's wrong (« intermod ×2: 2×… », « level … ») in the Note column.

26. Receiver filter and device profiles

What is the filter?

Right after the antenna, every receiver has an input filter (preselection) that only lets through a slice of spectrum around its frequency. Anything further away is strongly attenuated. In the calculation, as in common coordination software, the filter value applies on each side: with 16 MHz, for a carrier at 500 MHz, transmitters from 484 to 516 MHz count; with 32 MHz, those within ±32 MHz.

Why does it change the intermod calculation? A product (e.g. 2A − B) is made in the receiver's front end from the transmitters it receives strongly. If A is 40 MHz away, the filter has already cut it: no product. So: a product only bothers a frequency if ALL its transmitters are inside its receiver's filter.

  • The filter figure only says which slice of the spectrum gets into the receiver, hence how many transmitters count in the calculation (16 MHz makes fewer count than 32 MHz). It does not rank receivers.
  • The spacing (minimum distance between two carriers) and the tolerances (margin around an intermodulation product, per type: 2 TX, 3 TX, 5th order; 0 = type ignored) complete the profile.
  • None (0) = all of them count: the most careful choice when you don't know the device.
  • Products made in the transmitters themselves (in-ears on a combiner, antenna amplifier) are not filtered by the receiver: that's why the in-ear profiles also count the 5th order.

Built-in profiles

Importing a .ezrf3 plan

Your plan coordinated in your coordination software (.ezrf3 document) arrives as is in My frequencies: 📋 Prepare › 📥 Import a list and choose the .ezrf3 document (or drop it on the window). Another way: in your coordination software's frequency plan, select the rows, Ctrl+C, then 📋 Paste a list here.

  • Plan group → scene, section → group, with the zone in front of the scene name when there are several. Unnamed frequency → “Device #n · 1, 2…”.
  • 🗂 Sort the plan's stages: if your plan has one stage per set (“T2 - 111 15:00 - 15:40”, “T1 - WINDROSE 21:55 - 23:10”…), the import files them into their real stage by itself (“T2” = initials of “TERMINAL 2”) and the set becomes a group (“111 15:00 - 15:40 · IEMS”). The table lets you change everything row by row: target stage, group (the plan's sections, the set name or both); the preview follows. The sorting is kept when you follow the file.
  • 🏷 Names of unnamed frequencies: a frequency with no name in the plan takes the name of its device by default (“Shure SLX-D G58 #1 · 1”). Choose “Group name” to get “THE BROWNING · MICS 1” (scene prefix and times removed) or “Group + device”; the model stays in the note. A name written in the plan is always kept, and the choice is kept when you follow the file.
  • 🎬 Planning from the times: groups whose name contains times (“15:00 - 15:40”) can become Planning slots: outside its set, a switched-off group does not raise an ABSENT alarm.
  • With the .ezrf3 document, each device becomes a custom profile with its settings from the document (spacing, filter, 2 TX / 3 TX tolerances, 5th order if ticked on the device, step) and it is set on its group: Check the plan and Coordinate use its settings. With a copy-paste, devices are linked by name to your profiles.
  • The document's background scan goes into 📍 Scans by place; the noted interferences can be added as external transmitters; struck-out or out-of-service frequencies are ignored.
  • Each zone of the document is checked separately (for example one day per zone): to check a zone, choose “the active layer” in Check the plan.

🔗 Follow the file. When importing a .ezrf3, tick “Follow this file”: when you save it again in your coordination software (re-coordination during the festival), the app shows the frequencies added, moved or removed and you tick those you take (Ctrl+Z to go back). 📋 Prepare › 🔗 Followed plan: check now or stop following. The link is kept with the show.

Import and follow a WWB, WSM, Wisycom or DPA plan

Same way (📋 Prepare › 📥 Import, or drop the file on the window), same preview and same 🔗 Follow this file:

FileWhat is taken
Shure WWB .shw (show)the coordinated frequencies: channel name, zone = stage, series and band = group (“AD G56”). Channels all named “Shure” become “Shure 1, 2…”.
Shure .cug (group exported by WWB)the channels of the group (“AD G56 · 1, 2…”).
Sennheiser WSM .wsm (project)each receiver's frequency, group = receiver type, and its rules (carrier spacing, intermod tolerances, range) as a custom profile.
