The preview puts them in a “To complete” table: the frequency is found by name in your list (“DEP 1” ↔ “HF 1 DEPART”) or in another plan (📂 Look the names up…), otherwise you type it. It is kept with the file follow-up.
DPA N .acp (project)each channel's name and frequency, and the spacing of the chosen mode (600 / 500 / 400 kHz) as a custom profile.

Custom profiles

📋 Prepare › 🎛 Device profiles (or “✏ My profiles” in the plan check): ＋ New copies a profile, ＋ From current settings takes the window's settings. Name, filter, spacing, step, tolerances, note. Custom profiles are kept in your settings and in your shows. The filter of a device can depend on its band (e.g. group A of an evolution): make one profile per band if needed.

27. Line check

🎤 button or Ctrl+L: switch your transmitters on one by one; each frequency turns ✓ as soon as its signal arrives. A summary “14 / 16 OK, missing: …” goes into the log. An unknown signal right next to a missing frequency points to a pack set to the wrong channel.

28. Spectera / WMAS (wideband carriers)

  • 📋 Prepare › 📶 Add a block: TV channel or centre frequency + width (6 or 8 MHz). Or right-click a frequency › “Wide block”.
  • “Must transmit”: the median level of the block is used; “must stay free”: the peak.
  • Intermod and the plan check take the width of the blocks into account.

29. Two tinySAs, network relay

  1. ⚙ Settings › 2nd tinySA and names: tick “Use a 2nd tinySA” and give its port (COM4) or network address.
  2. On another PC: TinySA-Monitor.exe --relais (or 🔌 Hardware › 📡 Network relay), “Share”, then type the address shown (e.g. 192.168.1.20:5025) on the main PC.
  3. Bands table, “tinySA” column: Auto, 1 or 2. ✂ Split cuts a large band in two.
  4. Position names (Stage, FOH…): shown in the alarms (“seen by FOH”).
  5. ⚖ Calibrate the 2nd against the 1st: same signal into both (splitter), ~20 s, offset set automatically.

If one tinySA drops out, the other takes over all the bands (⚠ DEVICE). On a network, prefer a cable to Wi-Fi.

Up to 8 tinySAs: one per scene

On a big site, put one tinySA per scene (or per area): ⚙ Settings › Several tinySAs, “Other tinySAs (3rd to 8th)” table › ＋ Add a tinySA, then its name (“Stage B”), its address and possibly an offset. Address: a USB port (COM5, several tinySAs on a USB hub of the PC), a network address (192.168.1.23:5025, one Raspberry Pi per tinySA) or the name of a saved address.

  • Then attach each tinySA to its scene (📡 Scenes, or the bar above the spectrum): it sweeps all the bands where it is, and that scene's frequencies are judged with what it sees.
  • Several tinySAs on the same scene: the app keeps the best level (like diversity).
  • Without a scene, the tinySAs share the bands (shorter cycle), or all sweep everything in 🔀 Diversity.
  • ⚖ Calibrate: all tinySAs sweep the same band and each one is aligned on the 1st.
  • A tinySA that drops out: ⚠ DEVICE, the others take over its bands. The table is set while monitoring is stopped; Delete removes a row (the following tinySAs keep their scenes).

Home-made diversity: two antennas, the best of both

A diversity receiver listens to two antennas and keeps the better one: when one falls into a dip (someone in front, a reflection cancelling the signal), the other takes over. A single tinySA on a single antenna does not have that luck: it can see a mic “drop” while your receivers get it perfectly.

  1. Two tinySAs, each on its own antenna, the antennas a few metres apart (or one on each A / B branch of your antenna distribution).
  2. ⚖ First calibrate the 2nd against the 1st (same signal into both), so they read the same.
  3. ⚙ Settings › 2nd tinySA: tick 🔀 Diversity. Both then sweep the same bands (“tinySA” column: “1 + 2”) and, for each frequency, the app keeps the stronger level of the two.

Under the box, each tinySA's share (“best level: Stage 58 % · FOH 42 %”) shows that both are useful; in the log, an alarm names the tinySA that had the best level (“best: FOH”). The cycle is not shorter than with a single tinySA (each sweeps everything). Unticked, the two share the bands to go twice as fast. With two tinySAs attached to two different scenes, per-scene monitoring applies instead.

Several tinySAs on a single Raspberry Pi

Install the relay with sh install_pi.sh multi: each tinySA plugged into the Pi (powered USB hub beyond two) gets its own network port, 5025, 5026, 5027… It is recognised by its serial number: the same tinySA always keeps the same port. In the app, one address per tinySA: tinysa-sac.local:5025, tinysa-sac.local:5026… (details in the Raspberry Pi kit README).

Security. The relay has no password: keep it on the FOH technical network. On a shared Wi-Fi, only allow the FOH PC (TSM_RELAY_ALLOW= the PC's IP, see the kit README). A PC that freezes is dropped after 5 s and no longer blocks the relay.

Portable hunting kit: tinySA + Raspberry Pi + phone

The PC stays at the RF desk; you walk around with a tinySA plugged by USB into a Raspberry Pi (USB power bank), which shares it over Wi-Fi. Your phone shows the hunt and beeps. Only one tinySA: it goes in the bag, it is the 1st tinySA. Two tinySAs: one stays on the PC and monitors, the other goes in the bag (2nd tinySA).

  1. Get the kit: on the release page, next to the exe, the file relais-raspberry-pi.zip (relais folder: the Pi program tinysa_relais.py, its installer install_pi.sh and the step-by-step guide LISEZMOI.md, in French).
  2. Prepare the Pi (once): Raspberry Pi Imager › Raspberry Pi OS Lite; in its settings: hostname tinysa-sac, the RF desk Wi-Fi, user / password, SSH enabled.
  3. Install the relay (once), from the Windows Terminal, in the unzipped folder: scp -r relais tinysa-sac.local: then ssh tinysa-sac.local, then on the Pi cd relais and sh install_pi.sh. The relay then starts by itself at every boot and finds the tinySA by itself.
  4. On the PC: port list at the top › 🌐 Network tinySA: saved addresses… › ＋ Add (tinysa-sac.local or the Pi's IP address) › 🔌 Test › Use for the 1st tinySA (one tinySA) or for the 2nd (two tinySAs; position name « Backpack » in ⚙ Settings › 2nd tinySA and names). Then ▶ Start.
  5. On the phone: the web page (📣 Alerts and web page), 🔎 Hunt view. Type the frequency, pick the bag's tinySA, ▶ Hunt (web page PIN). The phone shows the level in large type and beeps (the PC stays quiet). With two tinySAs, the PC's one keeps monitoring all the bands.

The Pi changes address with the Wi-Fi: saved addresses

On each network (home Wi-Fi, festival network, phone hotspot) the Pi gets another IP address. Instead of typing it again each time, save one address per network in 🌐 Network tinySA: saved addresses… (at the bottom of the port list, in ⚙ Settings › Connections, or next to the 2nd tinySA's address):

  • a name and an address per row, for example « Pi · home » = 192.168.1.42, « Pi · festival » = 10.0.0.5, « Pi · phone » = 172.20.10.2 (port 5025 is added automatically);
  • 🔌 Test tries to reach the relay at each address: “answers” = the Pi is on, on this network, and its relay is running; “name not found” = this network does not know that name; “no answer” = wrong address or Pi off;
  • each address then shows up directly in the port list (« 🌐 Pi · festival — 10.0.0.5 ») and in the 2nd tinySA's list: switching network is one click;
  • the addresses and the chosen tinySA are saved with the show (🎪): reopening the festival's show brings back that festival's Pi address. The show's addresses are added to the PC's (same name: the show's wins).

Tip: the name tinysa-sac.local works on most networks whatever the IP; some event Wi-Fi networks block it: then keep a backup IP address in the list.

Advance coordination with the roaming tinySA (« Field » web view)

Before the festival, walk around the site with the kit and keep each stage's spectrum, from your phone. The view is hidden by default: tick « 🎒 Field » in 📣 Alerts and web page › offered views. Every command needs the web page PIN.

  1. 📍 Where is this tinySA? Tick the stage you are at (one, several, or ☑ All), then 📡 This tinySA is here. Its sweeps then feed those stages' spectrum.
  2. ↺ New scan here: the max hold restarts from zero (when you arrive somewhere new).
  3. Wait a few sweeps, then 💾 Keep this scan, with a label if you like (« stage left », « FOH », « dressing rooms »…). You can keep as many as you like per stage, on different stages.
  4. The « 📊 Kept scans » list shows them all; 🗑 deletes one.
  5. 📈 What the tinySA sees (in the Field view): the live spectrum with persistence (every sweep leaves a blue trace that fades over about fifteen sweeps: a signal that is always there draws a thick bright line, an intermittent one — walkie-talkie, hopping transmitter — a faint trace) and the max hold of each stage in its colour (« Max hold: … » list: all stages, one, or none). A stage's max hold = what the tinySA saw for it since the last ↺ New scan here: that is what 💾 keeps. The Persistence box also exists in the 📈 Spectrum view.

On the PC, clicking a stage in « My frequencies » shows the merge of its kept scans; 📍 Scans by location lists them all (WWB / WSM / CSV export).

Then, coordination per stage or global: in 🪄 Find N frequencies and 🆘 Backup frequency, the « Spectrum: … » list chooses what to avoid: one stage (all its kept scans + its current max hold), the whole site (merge of all scans, for frequencies that work everywhere) or the current max hold. If a stage is selected in « My frequencies », it is offered by default.

The Pi and the phone must stay within the site Wi-Fi coverage. Without Wi-Fi: the tinySA on its own, on its own screen (frequency in the centre, small span, marker on the peak), still works.

Network link status

For a network tinySA (Raspberry Pi, other PC), its throughput and response delay are shown next to its version, updated every 2 s (e.g. « 🌐 18 KB/s · 12 ms »). A tinySA uses a few tens of KB/s: the network is never saturated; a delay that climbs (hundreds of ms) points to a weak or crowded Wi-Fi.

30. Phone alerts and web page

Push alerts

  • 📣 button or 🎚 Monitor › 📣 Alerts: ntfy (free app, no account: subscribe to the channel name shown) or Telegram (bot from @BotFather; “🔎 Find my chat id” does it for you).
  • Alert language: same as the app, French or English.
  • Step-by-step 📖 guide, and “Send a test alert”. Internet is needed (4G, venue Wi-Fi). Wi-Fi with a login portal (hotel, festival) often blocks ntfy: switch the phone to 4G.

Web page for the team

  • Same window: enable the web page; the team opens the address shown (http://192.168.x.x:8080).
  • Views to choose from: list, wall, live spectrum, waterfall, alarms, 🎛 Control room. Optional password.
  • 🔎 Hunt: hunt an interferer from the phone (see « Portable hunting kit », chapter 29).
  • 🎛 Control room: the screen for the RF desk (tablet, TV). At the top, alarms in very large blinking text (or « ✔ All good »); below, one big status light per group (stage › group): green = all OK, orange = a weak signal or something to watch, red = an alarm, with the names involved. ⛶ Full screen, and the filter to show a single stage.
  • Everyone picks their own language (FR / EN button at the top of the page); by default, their phone's language.
  • List of connected people: rename, 👋 identify, disconnect everyone. Acknowledge from the phone with a PIN code.

Tech page: manage the server from a phone

📱 QR code (🎚 Monitor › Remote, or button in 📣 Alerts and web page): the team scans the code with the phone's camera and lands straight on the chosen view (home, wall, alarms, FOH, Tech…), without typing the address. “Save as PNG” to print it and stick it up at FOH.

The 🛠 Tech view (hidden until you tick it in 🔔 Alerts and web page › Shared views) lets the RF team drive the PC remotely: ▶ start / ■ stop, 🔕 silence, ✔ acknowledge all, 💾 save the show, set the thresholds, add / edit / remove a frequency and change its status, attach each tinySA to its stage, 👋 identify a tinySA, and see who is connected.

From the stage, on the phone: ⌨ Add mics accepts the same quick entry as the PC (“HF1 558.2, HF2 574”, or a pasted message), with the stage and group suggested as you type. On each mic, 🆘 asks for 3 replacement frequencies; tapping one replaces the mic (after confirming) and logs it on the PC.

  • Tech password (6 characters or more): different from the page password, give it only to the RF team. 5 wrong tries → locked 5 minutes.
  • Approval on the PC (“Approve each new device on this PC” box, ticked by default): even with the right password, a phone only gets access after your “Yes” in the window that opens on the PC.
  • Access lasts 12 h. In the connected list, 🛠 marks those who have it; Remove Tech access takes it back. Changing the Tech password removes it from everyone.
  • The page travels unencrypted on the network (no HTTPS): keep it on the production network.

31. Sessions, playback, report

Recording the session (offered at ▶ Start)

At every start, the app asks whether to record the whole session: the spectrum of every sweep, the log and your frequency list, into the folder of your choice (external drive, USB stick…), one sub-folder per session (date + show name). If something happens during the show, you can go back to it afterwards, even if the app was closed in between. The estimated disk space is shown (often a few dozen MB per hour).

  • 💾 Record and start, ▶ Start without recording or Cancel.
  • “Don't ask again” keeps your choice; the Ask at every start box (Log tab) brings the question back.
  • The session closes on its own at ▶ Stop.

⏪ Playback

  • ⏪ button: look at the spectrum at any moment: the last 30 minutes in memory, 📂 a recorded session (with its frequency list and log from that time) or 🕘 the last session.
  • Time slider, fast playback, “Go to” a log event, max hold since the start.
  • 💾 Export…: saves what is being played back (e.g. the last 30 minutes in memory) as a session, into the folder of your choice, to archive or send.

Compare two sessions

In the playback: ⚖ Compare with a session… overlays the max hold of another session (soundcheck, yesterday…) as purple dots, and lists the extra (new here) or missing signals compared with it. Handy to see what came with the audience or another stage.

Occupancy by hour (risky time slots)

Playback › 📊, 📊 Analyse, or ☰ More. A table: one row per frequency, one column per hour, the % of the time it was above the « busy » threshold. For a frequency that must transmit, that's normal; for a « must stay free » reserve, it's a risky time slot (red cell, summary at the bottom). Hover over a cell for details.

Show report

📊 Analyse › 📄 Report: standalone HTML (alarms, occupancy, log), printable to PDF.

32. The log

  • Log tab: everything that happens, newest at the top; Auto log = one CSV per day.
  • 📝 What to log…: tick the kinds of events to keep: alarms (CONFLICT, INTERMOD, MISSING), TOO STRONG, frequency switching on (BUSY), back to normal, unknown signals, tinySA lost / found, operations (line check, new frequency). Alarms still go off: only the log is filtered.
  • A busy spell shorter than 3 s (a signal hovering around the threshold) is not logged: it is counted in the note of the next “BUSY” (“+ N pass(es) shorter than 3 s before”). A 💤 switched off (I know) mic no longer fills the log.
  • Double-click an “UNKNOWN”: adds it to your list.

33. Appearance and language

Settings ( button at the top, Ctrl+,)

  • 🖥 General: language, interface (ultra simple / simple / expert), level unit, colours and themes, words of the Signal column.
  • 🔊 Sound: alarm sounds on / off, app sounds (3 notes = critical, 2 = normal, 1 = info) or Windows beep, choice of audio output (sound card, headphones, HDMI speaker, audio interface…), volume, buttons to listen. The interference hunt beep comes out the same way.
  • 📁 Files: logs and reports folder, recorded sessions folder, « ask at each start », shows folder.
  • 🔗 Connections: phone alerts and web page, festival mode, network relay, diagnostics.
  • ☰ More › 🎨 Appearance and language › 🎨 Colours and themes: Pro dark (default), Pro light, Catppuccin, Tokyo Night, Dracula, Rosé Pine, Gruvbox, Nord; for colour-blind users, one theme per type: Colour-blind · deuteranopia (green), · protanopia (red), · tritanopia (blue / yellow) and Monochrome (no colour); High contrast; the Analyser range (green, blue, amber, white) and Night (red), with a spectrum like an old CRT analyser; or every colour by hand. The state is always written out in the Signal cell: colour is only a help.
  • 🏷 Statuses, 🔤 Words and colours of the Signal column.
  • 🌐 Language / Langue: Français or English; the app offers to restart. On the very first start it follows the Windows language.
Part E — Help

34. Frequently asked questions

The PC does not see the tinySA.

In order: is the tinySA on? does the cable carry data (try another)? is tinySA-App closed? ⟳ next to the port. A tinySA in « USB disk » mode (SD menu) is not a serial port: leave that mode.

The spectrum is empty / flat.

Antenna screwed on? Right band ticked (📶 Bands)? Demo mode unticked if you have a real tinySA? Hover: a level around −100 dBm everywhere = the antenna picks up nothing (wrong socket or antenna unplugged).

I get lots of false CONFLICT alarms.

The « busy » threshold is too low (in the noise): click Auto, or raise it a few dB. An LED screen or a power supply near the tinySA also raises the noise: move it away.

My mic is on but stays ABSENT.

Check that the list frequency is exactly the transmitter's (to the kHz), that the band containing it is ticked, and that the transmitter is not too far from the tinySA (level under the « weak » threshold).

I click a stage and the live spectrum is empty.

No tinySA is attached to that stage (a tinySA attached elsewhere only feeds its own stages). An orange banner says so above the spectrum, with who watches what: click « 📡 The 1st tinySA is here » (it moves to this stage) or « 🌐 Whole site ». In « My frequencies », « 📡 name » next to a stage shows the tinySA watching it; ∅ No stage (My tinySA and their stages) puts it back on the whole site.

Sweeping is slow.

Fewer bands, ⚡ Points on « Auto fast », or a 2nd tinySA. Live zoom only sweeps a small area, very fast.

What is the difference between max hold, persistence and a kept scan?

Max hold keeps the highest level seen since the last Reset (in memory). Persistence (web page) shows what comes back often, fading out. A kept scan is a max hold saved in the show, for a stage, for coordination and the report.

Per-stage or global coordination?

Per stage if the stages are far apart and the equipment does not move: more frequencies available. Global for equipment that moves around (presenters, walkies) or a compact site: frequencies that work everywhere.

The calculations say « problem » but my coordination software says OK.

Intermod rules and profiles differ from one program to another. Choose your device's profile and the « Standard » rules; the receiver filter changes the result a lot (Filter chapter).

The Raspberry Pi kit does not see the tinySA.

USB-C data cable, tinySA on, the Pi's USB-A socket (the Pi 4's USB-C socket only powers it). On the Pi: python3 /opt/tinysa-relais/tinysa_relais.py --diag tells you what is missing.

Can I use the app in English?

Yes: ☰ More › 🌐 Langue / Language, then restart. The web page is chosen per person (FR / EN button).

35. Troubleshooting

ProblemWhat to do
Port not found / “access denied”Close tinySA-App (one program at a time), replug the USB, ⟳ button next to the port.
The tinySA stops answering after a whileThe app retries on its own. After 3 failed attempts: unplug / replug the tinySA (it can freeze, also with tinySA-App).
A band does not fill up🔌 Hardware › 🩺 Diagnostics, and send the file.
Lots of false alarms“Busy” threshold too low: raise it (or Auto), check the carpet with ❓ Traces; an overloaded tinySA makes up signals: move it away from the transmitters.

The app crashedSend %APPDATA%\TinySAMonitor\crash.log. The settings are saved every minute, with a backup copy.

36. Glossary

Every word of RF and of the app, explained simply. The same glossary is in the app (☰ More › Help › 📚 Glossary), with a search.

WordMeaning
HFHere: everything that goes over the air (wireless mics, in-ears, walkie-talkies). In the trade, « RF » means all the wireless links of a show.
Frequency (MHz)The « slot » where a device transmits, in megahertz. Two mics on the same frequency interfere. Example: 606.500 MHz. Show mics mostly sit between 470 and 694 MHz (UHF).
SpectrumThe app's graph: frequencies from left to right, received power from bottom to top. A transmitter makes a « bump » (a peak) at its frequency.
dBmThe unit of received power. The bigger the number (closer to 0), the stronger: −40 dBm is very strong, −90 dBm is weak, −110 dBm is noise. +10 dB = 10 times more power.
dBµVAnother level unit, used by some software (Wisycom…). dBµV = dBm + 107.
Noise floorThe minimum level the tinySA sees even without any transmitter: its own noise plus the venue's (LED screens, lighting…). Anything clearly above the floor is a signal.
SweepThe tinySA measures one frequency after another, from left to right: one full pass is called a sweep. It lasts from under a second to several seconds depending on width and number of points.
PointsThe number of measurements per sweep. More points = more detail but slower. « ⚡ Auto » picks a good compromise by itself.
RBWThe « fineness » of each measurement (width of the tinySA's filter). Narrow = sees small close signals but slow; wide = fast but two close signals merge. Leave it on Auto if you are starting out.
Max holdThe orange curve: the highest level seen at each frequency since the last « Reset max ». It keeps track of a transmitter even if it was only on for a second.
Peak holdThe name of max hold in simple mode: the orange curve, the highest level seen at each frequency since “Clear peaks”.
PersistenceEach sweep leaves a trace that slowly fades, like on an analyser: what is often there glows, what rarely passes leaves a faint trace (app spectrum, ⋯ button, and Spectrum / Field web views).
Auto thresholdOne threshold per frequency = its local noise floor + a margin (+ 12 dB by default), drawn dashed. On a DTT channel the local floor is the DTT: the threshold rises with it, so a mic placed in that channel stays monitored (ABSENT). Full sheet: ❓ button next to « Auto ».
“Busy” thresholdThe red line: above it, a frequency is considered busy (someone is transmitting). « Auto » places it a bit above the noise floor.
« Weak » thresholdBelow the busy threshold: a signal above this level but under « busy » is « weak » (distant transmitter, weak battery, or rising noise).
Must transmit (In use)Status of a frequency where YOUR transmitter must be on. If it goes quiet for too long: ABSENT alarm.
Must stay free (Free)Status of a frequency you keep in reserve (backup, another day's frequency…). If a signal shows up there: CONFLICT alarm.
MISSINGAlarm: a transmitter that must transmit is no longer seen (flat battery, transmitter off, antenna unplugged, artist too far).
CONFLICTAlarm: a signal appeared on a frequency that had to stay free (another team, a jammer, intermodulation).
AcknowledgeTelling an alarm « I've seen it »: the sound stops, the alarm stays displayed as long as the problem lasts.
Intermodulation (IM)When several transmitters are close together, they create « ghost frequencies » by arithmetic (e.g. 2 × A − B). If a ghost lands on one of your mics, it interferes. Coordination is mostly about avoiding that.
IM3 / IM5Intermodulation order: 3rd order (2A − B, A + B − C) is the strongest and most annoying, 5th order (3A − 2B…) is weaker.
CoordinationChoosing the frequencies of all devices so that none interferes with another: enough spacing between them, no intermodulation on them, away from what already occupies the venue.
Frequency planThe final list of frequencies of all your devices, once coordinated.
Spacing (separation)The minimum distance between two carriers so they do not interfere (e.g. 300 to 500 kHz depending on the devices).
Receiver filterThe slice of spectrum that enters the receiver around its frequency (preselection, e.g. 16 MHz: transmitters within ±16 MHz count). For the calculation, only transmitters in this slice can create intermod in this receiver. This number alone does not say whether a receiver is good: its robustness is set by the profile's spacing and tolerances.
Device profileThe coordination settings of a brand / range (spacing, filter, tolerances, step). Pick yours so the calculations match.
Step (increment)The frequencies a device can use go step by step (e.g. 25 kHz): coordination only suggests frequencies your device can be set to.
CarrierA transmitter's signal at its frequency (the peak on the spectrum).
Wide block (WMAS, Spectera)Some recent digital systems use a whole 6 to 8 MHz channel instead of a single frequency: on the spectrum, a plateau instead of a peak.
DTTDigital terrestrial television: 8 MHz plateaus in the UHF band. These channels are taken and must be avoided (TV channel strip under the spectrum).
UHFThe 470–694 MHz band (in France) where most show mics work, shared with DTT.
Stage / groupHow your frequencies are sorted: a stage = a venue or a set, a group = a set of devices (mics, in-ears, walkies…). Optional but handy at a festival.
Kept scanA saved spectrum (the max hold at a given time and place): it is the venue's memory and is used for coordination.
MergeCombining several scans: the strongest level of each is kept, to see the worst case of the whole site.
Roaming tinySAA tinySA carried from stage to stage (in a bag, with a Raspberry Pi) to scan each location, while the PC stays at the FOH.
RelayThe small program that shares a tinySA over the network (on a Raspberry Pi or another PC), so the app sees it remotely.
Line checkBefore the show: each transmitter is switched on one after the other and the app ticks those it sees, to check that everything is there.
SessionThe recording of everything the app saw during monitoring, to review it afterwards (replay).
Show (🎪)A file holding all your work for an event (frequencies, stages, bands, scans…), to reopen the following year.

The coordination tools are hidden at first: 📋 Prepare › “🔒 Coordination tools hidden: show them…” opens ⚙ Settings › General, box “Coordination tools (advanced)”. 39. Where are my files?

Shure Wireless Workbench (WWB), Sennheiser WSM, Wisycom Manager, Soundbase and tinySA are trademarks of their owners. TinySA Monitor is neither affiliated with nor endorsed by them; their names are only used to say which files it is compatible with.

  • Settings: %APPDATA%\TinySAMonitor\ (config.json + config.json.bak, reference.json, crash.log).
  • Shows: Documents\TinySA Monitor\Shows\ (.tsashow files).
  • Logs, reports, diagnostics: Documents\TinySA Monitor\Journaux\ (can be changed).
  • Recorded sessions: the folder chosen at start (default Journaux\enregistrements\), one sub-folder per session: chunk_*.npz slices, session.json, journal.csv.
